questions.stem: What distinguishes instruction tuning from ordinary supervised fine-tuning on a single task?
choices: It uses reinforcement learning
It trains on many tasks phrased as instructions with their responses, teaching the model to follow instructions in general rather than to perform one task
It requires no labelled data
It only adjusts the embedding layer
questions.explanation: Instruction tuning generalises the objective: by training across a broad mixture of instruction-response pairs, the model learns the behaviour of following instructions, which then transfers to instructions it has never seen. Single-task fine-tuning produces a specialist instead. It is still supervised learning, not RL.

questions.stem: What does a reward model learn to do?
choices: Generate better responses directly
Score a response so that its output correlates with human preference, providing a signal that can be optimised against
Classify prompts by topic
Compress the base model
questions.explanation: A reward model is a scorer, typically trained on pairs where a human marked one response better than another. It converts sparse, expensive human judgement into a cheap differentiable signal that an optimiser can consult millions of times. It never generates anything itself.

questions.stem: Reward models are usually trained on pairwise comparisons rather than absolute scores. Why?
choices: Pairwise data is cheaper to store
Humans judge 'which of these two is better' far more consistently than they assign an absolute number, so the labels are less noisy
Absolute scores cannot be used in a loss function
Pairwise comparison requires no annotators
questions.explanation: Absolute ratings drift between annotators and within one annotator over time, so a 7 from one person is not a 7 from another. Relative comparisons are stable and are what the standard ranking loss consumes. It is a measurement decision, not a storage one.

questions.stem: In what sense is a language model treated as a policy in RLHF?
choices: It enforces content policy rules
Its conditional distribution over next tokens is the policy: given a state (the context) it assigns probabilities to actions (tokens)
It stores the training policy in its weights
It governs which users may call it
questions.explanation: Framing generation as sequential decision-making is what lets reinforcement learning apply: context is state, the next token is an action, and the model's distribution is the policy to be improved. The reward arrives at the end of a generated sequence.

questions.stem: What are the three stages of a classic RLHF pipeline, in order?
choices: Reward modelling, supervised fine-tuning, then PPO
Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, reward-model training on preference comparisons, then policy optimisation against the reward model
PPO, supervised fine-tuning, then evaluation
Pretraining, quantisation, then deployment
questions.explanation: SFT first gives a model that already responds sensibly, which makes the samples used for preference collection worth comparing. The reward model is then fit to those comparisons, and finally RL optimises the policy against it. Reversing the first two stages would mean collecting preferences over incoherent output.

questions.stem: Why does PPO include a KL penalty against the reference (pre-RL) model?
choices: To speed up convergence
To keep the policy from drifting far from the original distribution, which would let it exploit the reward model and produce degenerate high-scoring text
To reduce GPU memory
To normalise the reward scale
questions.explanation: The reward model is an imperfect proxy, and an unconstrained policy will find inputs that score highly while being useless — the classic reward-hacking failure. Penalising divergence from the reference keeps the policy in the region where the reward model was trained and remains meaningful.

questions.stem: What does the 'proximal' in proximal policy optimization refer to?
choices: The proximity of the reward model to the policy model in memory
Constraining each update so the new policy stays close to the previous one, via a clipped objective, which keeps training stable
Training on nearby tokens only
The distance between training and inference hardware
questions.explanation: Policy-gradient methods can take a catastrophically large step from a lucky batch. PPO clips the probability ratio between new and old policies so no single update moves the policy far, trading some sample efficiency for much greater stability.

questions.stem: Which TWO components must be held in memory during a PPO run, beyond the policy being trained?
choices: The reward model, to score generated responses
The frozen reference model, to compute the KL penalty
The original pretraining corpus
The tokenizer of a different model family
questions.explanation: PPO's memory cost is a common surprise: the trainable policy, a frozen reference for the KL term, and the reward model must all be resident, often alongside a value head. That multiplied footprint is a large part of why DPO became attractive.

questions.stem: What is the central claim of direct preference optimization (DPO)?
choices: Preferences can be learned without any human data
The RLHF objective can be reparameterised so the optimal policy is obtained directly from preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss, removing the separate reward model and the RL loop
PPO is mathematically invalid
Preferences must be converted to absolute scores first
questions.explanation: DPO shows the reward model is implicit in the policy itself under the standard RLHF formulation, so the preference data can update the policy directly. That removes reward-model training, sampling and the RL machinery, leaving a stable supervised-style objective over the same human data.

questions.stem: Why does the partition function matter in the derivation of DPO?
choices: It sets the learning rate
It is the intractable normalising constant of the optimal policy, and the derivation cancels it by working with the ratio between chosen and rejected responses
It counts the training partitions
It determines the batch size
questions.explanation: The optimal RLHF policy has a closed form containing a normalising constant that cannot be computed. Because the loss compares a chosen response against a rejected one for the same prompt, that constant appears in both terms and cancels — which is exactly what makes the objective tractable.

questions.stem: Which TWO are practical advantages of DPO over PPO-based RLHF?
choices: No separate reward model needs to be trained and held in memory
Training is more stable, being a supervised-style objective rather than an RL loop with sampling
It needs less preference data than PPO
It guarantees better final quality in every case
questions.explanation: The operational gains are real: fewer models resident, no rollout sampling, and far fewer things to go wrong. Both methods consume the same preference pairs, and which yields better final quality is task-dependent rather than settled.

questions.stem: In the course's sentiment-steering example, what role does a sentiment classifier play?
choices: It replaces the language model
It acts as the reward function, scoring generated responses so the policy can be optimised toward the desired sentiment
It tokenises the input
It evaluates perplexity
questions.explanation: Any function that scores a response can serve as a reward, and an off-the-shelf sentiment classifier is a convenient stand-in for a learned reward model when demonstrating the mechanics. It makes the reward concrete and inspectable while the RLHF loop stays identical.

questions.stem: An RLHF-tuned model scores highly on the reward model but users find its answers evasive and padded. What is happening?
choices: The learning rate was too low
Reward hacking: the policy has found features the reward model rewards that do not correspond to genuine quality
The tokenizer is mismatched
The KL penalty is too strong
questions.explanation: A proxy optimised hard enough stops tracking the thing it proxied. Hedging and padding are classic artefacts because they are hard to mark wrong. The countermeasures are a stronger KL constraint, refreshing the reward model on new comparisons, and holding out human evaluation the optimiser never sees.

questions.stem: Why is LoRA frequently combined with RLHF or DPO training?
choices: It improves the reward model's accuracy
It cuts the trainable parameters and optimiser state dramatically, which matters when several large models must be resident at once
It removes the need for preference data
It makes the KL penalty unnecessary
questions.explanation: Alignment training is memory-bound because policy, reference and reward models share the device. Training only low-rank adapters shrinks the optimiser state for the trainable part, often making the difference between fitting on available hardware and not.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a held-out preference set during alignment training?
choices: To increase the training signal
To measure whether improvements generalise rather than reflecting overfitting to the preference data the model was optimised on
To compute the KL penalty
To initialise the reward model
questions.explanation: Both the reward model and the policy can overfit the comparisons they saw. A held-out split, never used for either, shows whether the alignment gains extend to new preferences. Without it, rising training reward is indistinguishable from memorisation.

questions.stem: What does the TRL library provide?
choices: A tokenizer implementation
Trainers for the alignment stack — supervised fine-tuning, reward modelling, PPO and DPO — built on top of Transformers
A vector database
A dataset annotation interface
questions.explanation: TRL supplies SFTTrainer, RewardTrainer, PPOTrainer and DPOTrainer, mirroring the stages of the alignment pipeline so each can be run without reimplementing the algorithm. It sits on Transformers and integrates with PEFT for adapter-based training.

questions.stem: Which ordering of interventions is most cost-effective when a model's answers are unhelpful in a specific style?
choices: Go straight to RLHF
Try prompting, then supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, and only reach for preference-based alignment if the requirement is genuinely about preference between plausible answers
Start with DPO then fall back to prompting
Pretrain from scratch
questions.explanation: Each step up the ladder costs more and is harder to reverse. Prompting is instant, SFT teaches a demonstrable target behaviour, and preference methods are for the case where you cannot write the right answer but can tell which of two is better. Matching the method to the shape of the problem is the whole skill.

questions.stem: Why is the reference model frozen during PPO rather than updated alongside the policy?
choices: To save memory
Because it defines the fixed anchor the KL penalty measures against; if it moved with the policy, the constraint would permit unlimited cumulative drift
Because it has different weights initially
Because it is a smaller model
questions.explanation: The KL term is only meaningful relative to a fixed distribution. A reference that tracked the policy would always find it close by, and the penalty would stop constraining anything as the policy wandered arbitrarily far from where it began.
